name: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 2

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive sensory neuropathy typically presenting in infancy or early childhood, earlier than HSAN1
Caused by mutations in genes including WNK1 (the HSN2 exon/transcript), FAM134B/RETREG1, KIF1A and SCN9A depending on the subtype
There is severe, often global loss of all sensory modalities affecting distal limbs, causing painless injuries, ulcers, whitlows and acral mutilation
Sensory loss tends to be more diffuse and less strictly length-dependent than in HSAN1, and can involve the trunk
Autonomic disturbance is variable and generally less severe than in familial dysautonomia
Deep tendon reflexes are reduced or absent and there may be mild distal motor involvement
Nerve conduction studies show markedly reduced or absent sensory responses; biopsy reveals loss of myelinated and unmyelinated sensory fibres
Management is supportive, focused on protecting insensate limbs, preventing and treating ulcers and infections, and injury education
reference.pathophysiology: HSAN2 is a recessively inherited disorder of sensory neuron development and maintenance. Depending on the causative gene, the defect impairs axonal transport, endoplasmic reticulum shaping or sensory neuron survival: for example, the HSN2 nervous-system-specific transcript of WNK1 and mutations in FAM134B/RETREG1, KIF1A or SCN9A each disrupt the integrity of small and large sensory fibres. The result is early, profound loss of cutaneous sensation with relatively variable autonomic involvement, so affected children sustain repeated unperceived trauma leading to ulceration, infection and mutilating acral injury.
additionalDifferentials: Other HSAN subtypes, particularly HSAN1 (later onset, dominant) and familial dysautonomia
Leprosy and other infective neuropathies in endemic settings
Non-accidental injury when acral wounds are unexplained
Diabetic or other acquired sensory neuropathies in older patients
Syringomyelia and other central causes of dissociated sensory loss
additionalInvestigations: Targeted genetic testing of HSAN2-associated genes (WNK1/HSN2, FAM134B, KIF1A, SCN9A) and gene panels
Nerve conduction studies demonstrating absent or markedly reduced sensory responses
Skin biopsy or sural nerve biopsy showing loss of sensory fibres
Autonomic function testing to gauge the degree of autonomic involvement
Imaging of affected limbs to assess osteomyelitis, fractures or joint destruction
Exclusion of acquired and infective causes as appropriate
redFlags: Osteomyelitis or deep infection complicating a painless wound
Charcot joints or unrecognised fractures from repeated trauma
Corneal injury or ulceration from impaired protective sensation
Systemic sepsis from an infected mutilating lesion
reference.prognosis: HSAN2 is a lifelong disorder; the sensory deficit is largely static or slowly progressive, and with vigilant protective care many patients avoid major mutilation, though recurrent injuries, infections and amputations cause significant morbidity.
pitfalls: Mistaking recurrent acral injuries in a child for non-accidental injury and delaying diagnosis
Assuming a length-dependent pattern and overlooking the more diffuse sensory loss of HSAN2
Neglecting protective education and foot/hand care that prevent mutilating complications
Overlooking corneal and other non-limb sites vulnerable to unperceived injury
references: GeneReviews: Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy Type 2
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Provide vigilant lifelong protective care of the hands and feet from infancy, with skin inspection, protective footwear and gloves, and oral protection to prevent self-injury
Treat ulcers, whitlows and acral infections promptly with wound care, offloading and antibiotics for osteomyelitis
Manage fractures, joint destruction and Charcot arthropathy orthopaedically while avoiding unnecessary amputation
Educate children and caregivers on injury avoidance and early recognition of unperceived trauma
Address any autonomic disturbance symptomatically and monitor for its progression
Refer to multidisciplinary paediatric neurology, podiatry and orthopaedics, and offer genetic counselling given autosomal recessive inheritance
